From The Drug Czar’s 8-Year Plan to the Republican’s Drug-Free Century Act,
The Prohibitionist Agenda Is War Without End. Orwell Would Understand.
Analysis By Richard Cowan

One of the main features of the world of Orwell’s 1984 was endless war. From time to time the enemy would change and history would be rewritten so that today’s enemy had always been the enemy, but the important thing was that the war continued. The war was never intended to be won. On the contrary, it was a means to an end that had to continue forever. So it is with the WAR ON DRUGS.

The Drug Czar has recently taken to saying that he doesn’t like to call it a "war." War sounds bad.

Of course, the violence will continue. The taking of huge numbers of prisoners will continue. The seizure of property will continue. The massive prohibitionist propaganda will continue at wartime levels. He just doesn’t want to call it war.

Even there, Orwell anticipated him. "WAR IS PEACE!" -- proclaimed Big Brother.

Today, Vice President Al ("I inhaled for years.") Gore and the Drug Czar announced a "new" plan, which the AP called "a blend of strategies aimed at reducing the use and availability of drugs by 25 percent by 2002 and 50 percent by 2007."

The AP report goes on to explain that "Achieving the goal would mean just 3 percent of the U.S. population aged 12 and over would be using illegal drugs. The current figure is estimated at 6.4 percent. In 1979, the rate was near 15 percent."

Orwell: "Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past."

What neither the Drug Czar nor the AP tells us is that these numbers primarily reflect a reduction in reported marijuana use. Moreover, they absolutely ignore the fact that there was a crack cocaine epidemic in the midst of this great victory, and we are now seeing a major resurgence of heroin use, and various forms of speed are replacing crack in the stimulant market.

The AP also reports that the Drug Czar says that "Additional goals for the period ending in 2007 are to reduce by 30 percent the rate of crime associated with drug trafficking and use, and cutting the health and social costs associated with drugs by 25 percent."

Isn’t that interesting. A 50% drop in "drug use" will only reduce crime by 30% and "health and social costs associated with drugs by 25 percent." ???

Perhaps this is an acknowledgement that reducing marijuana use has little impact on crime or on health and social costs. Actually, reducing marijuana use may have just the opposite impact. But we will never know. The AP won't ask.

Orwell: "Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted all else follows."

The report also says that "As of 1995, the social costs of drug use were estimated at $110 billion, a 64 percent increase over 1990." This number begs for an explanation. How did the "social cost of drug use" rise by 64% in just five years? How did they measure this? Again, the AP won't ask.

Orwell again: "How can I help seeing what is in front of my eyes? Two plus two are four." To which Winston Smith’s mentor/tormentor replied, "Sometimes, Winston. Sometimes they are five. Sometimes they are three. Sometimes they are all of them at once. You must try harder. It is not easy to become sane."

The AP has already learned its lessons. The numbers are whatever the Ministry of Truth says they are.

Another feature of 1984 was "the memory hole." Handy device. Whenever the Ministry of Plenty missed a production target the old target just disappeared into the memory hole.

Fanciful? Not really. The Omnibus Crime Act of 1988 declared that DEAland would be "drug-free" by 1994. You will never read about that. It went down the memory hole. They must have one at the AP. Or maybe I am right in saying that marijuana prohibition causes long-term memory loss. Take your pick.

But it gets worse. The Senate Republicans seem intent on proving another feature of 1984, "If human equality is to be forever averted – if the High, as we have called them, are to keep their places permanently -- the prevailing mental condition must be controlled insanity."

How else can one explain Senate Bill 5: "The Drug-Free Century Act"? Century? Yes, century. This little jewel has such features of controlled insanity as

It says that "The Administrator shall make a grant to the Parent Collaboration to conduct a national campaign to build a new parent and family movement to help parents and families prevent drug abuse among their children."

In other words, it is funding prohibitionist propaganda to lobby for more prohibitionist propaganda to increase the power of the state to take children away from their parents in the name of the family. Doublethink.

"Parent Collaboration" is a subsidiary of National Families in Action, the Atlanta-based prohibitionist propaganda organization.

Check out their web sites: http://www.emory.edu/NFIA/about/partners/collaboration.html

Not only are they primarily focused on marijuana, they are heavily into reefer madness. They follow the party line that medical marijuana is a "scam" to "legalize drugs." Of course, that is why they get government funding.

The Drug-Free Century Act explicitly blames the marijuana reform movement for the increase in marijuana use:

"Three forces appeared to be driving this escalation in drug use among children and young adults. Between 1972 and 1978, a nationwide political campaign conducted by drug legalization advocates persuaded eleven state legislatures to `decriminalize' marijuana. (Many of those states have subsequently `recriminalized' the drug.)
(Marijuananews note: This is incorrect. Only, one state has recriminalized. Also note the term "drug legalization advocates" for the marijuana reform movement.)
Such legislative action reinforced advocates' assertion that marijuana was `relatively harmless.'
See

(5) The decriminalization effort gave rise to the emergence of `head shops' (shops for `heads,' or drug users--`coke heads,' `pot heads,' `acid heads,' etc.) which sold drug paraphernalia--an array of toys, implements, and instructional pamphlets and booklets to enhance the use of illicit drugs. Some 30,000 such shops were estimated to be doing business throughout the nation by 1978.

(6) In the absence of Federal funding for drug education then, most of the drug education materials that were available proclaimed that few illicit drugs were addictive and most were `less harmful' than alcohol and tobacco and therefore taught young people how to use marijuana, cocaine, and other illicit drugs `responsibly'.

(7) Between 1977 and 1980, three national parent drug-prevention organizations--National Families in Action, PRIDE, and the National Federation of Parents for Drug-Free Youth (now called the National Family Partnership)--emerged to help concerned parents form some 4,000 local parent prevention groups across the nation to reverse all of these trends in order to prevent children from using drugs. Their work created what has come to be known as the parents drug-prevention movement, or more simply, the parent movement. This movement set three goals: to prevent the use of any illegal drug, to persuade those who had started using drugs to stop, and to obtain treatment for those who had become addicted so that they could return to drug-free lives.

(8) The parent movement pursued a number of objectives to achieve these goals. First, it helped parents educate themselves about the harmful effects of drugs, teach that information to their children, communicate that they expected their children not to use drugs, and establish consequences if children failed to meet that expectation. Second, it helped parents form groups with other parents to set common age-appropriate social and behavioral guidelines to protect their children from exposure to drugs. Third, it encouraged parents to insist that their communities reinforce parents' commitment to protect children from drug use.

(9) The parent movement stopped further efforts to decriminalize marijuana, both in the states and at the Federal level

(10) The parent movement worked for laws to ban the sale of drug paraphernalia. If drugs were illegal, it made no sense to condone the sale of toys and implements to enhance the use of illegal drugs, particularly when those products targeted children."

While the bill often uses the generic term "drugs," it is quite clear that it is primarily focused on marijuana. As noted, it even implies that alcohol and tobacco are less harmful than marijuana. Like the prohibitionist propaganda groups that it would fund, the bill even attacks supporters of hemp.

Of course, the one thing that The Drug-Free Century Act does not mention is the projected number of arrests during the Drug-Free Century.

As economists like to say, if present trends continue, the Drug-Free Century will see between 75 million and 100 million arrests for marijuana alone.
See
1997 Marijuana Arrests Hit 695,000 -- A New Record; Percentage Of Marijuana Arrests For Simple Possession Ties 1979 Record -- Analysis By Richard Cowan

All of this is necessary to suppress medical marijuana. Why? The objective is Power for the sake of Power.

Orwell: "He took up his pen again and wrote: I understand HOW: I do not understand WHY."

The other day a very bright young reader wrote and said that he did not understand why the prohibitionists have to lie about everything. Most prohibitionists are not anywhere near power. They are like the fanatic in 1984 who was pleased when his own children turned him in for Thoughtcrimes, even though he was the most loyal of followers. Since he was arrested he had to be guilty! If he doubted it, his act of doubting would make him guilty of Thoughtcrime. It is just that simple.

Orwell: "How does one man assert his power over another, Winston?"

Winston thought. "By making him suffer," he said. "Exactly. By making him suffer. Obedience is not enough. Unless he is suffering, how can you be sure that he is obeying your will and not his own? Power is in inflicting pain and humiliation."

Consider the absurd humiliation inflicted on medical marijuana patients who are arrested.

People cannot be allowed to think for themselves. People cannot be allowed to alleviate their own pain outside of government approved channels. Doctors who try to help their patients get medical marijuana will be punished by denying them the right to prescribe even the approved pain relievers.

Orwell: "The old civilizations claimed that they were founded on love and justice. Ours is founded on hatred…. No one dares trust a wife or a child or a friend any longer."
See
PBS Frontline Program Snitch Gives Devastating Critique Of Drug War
On Both Television And The Internet

Orwell: "But always… there will be the intoxication of power."

The intoxication of power is one addiction that the authors of The Drug-Free Century Act will not prohibit.
